subject: History
description: Covers August Offer, Permanent Settlement, Subsidiary Alliance, and Doctrine of Lapse.

questions.stem: In the context of the Indian Freedom Struggle, the 'August Offer' of 1940 was proposed by which British Viceroy?

options.option_text: Lord Linlithgow
Lord Mountbatten
Lord Irwin
Lord Wavell

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Lord Linlithgow made the "August Offer" in 1940 to secure Indian cooperation in World War II after the fall of France to Nazi Germany. It offered Dominion Status (for the first time explicitly), expansion of the Viceroy's executive council to include more Indians, and the setting up of a constituent assembly after the war.
DECOY BUSTING: Irwin is associated with the 1931 Gandhi-Irwin Pact. Wavell proposed the Wavell Plan in 1945. Mountbatten was the last Viceroy who oversaw partition in 1947.
EXAM INSIGHT: Both the Congress and the Muslim League rejected the August Offer. The Congress launched the "Individual Satyagraha" (with Vinoba Bhave as the first Satyagrahi) in protest to show that India was not a willing party to the war.

questions.stem: Which brutal economic policy, introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793, gave Zamindars absolute ownership of land and fixed the revenue demand of the British East India Company in perpetuity?

options.option_text: The Permanent Settlement
The Ryotwari System
The Mahalwari System
The Subsidiary Alliance

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Permanent Settlement (or Zamindari System) was introduced by Cornwallis in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. It declared Zamindars (previously just tax collectors) as absolute owners of the land, provided they paid a fixed, permanent revenue to the British (10/11th to the British, 1/11th kept by the Zamindar). This reduced the actual cultivators to mere tenants.
DECOY BUSTING: The Ryotwari System (introduced by Thomas Munro in Madras/Bombay) collected revenue directly from the 'Ryot' (peasant). The Mahalwari System (Holt Mackenzie in NWFP) collected from the village headman. Subsidiary Alliance was a political/military treaty system introduced by Wellesley.
EXAM INSIGHT: Under the "Sunset Clause" of this settlement, if a Zamindar failed to deposit the revenue by sunset on a specified date, his entire estate was auctioned off.

questions.stem: The system of 'Subsidiary Alliance' was used extensively to bring Indian princely states under British paramountcy without direct war. Who pioneered this policy in India?

options.option_text: Lord Wellesley
Lord Dalhousie
Lord Hastings
Warren Hastings

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Lord Wellesley (Viceroy 1798-1805) perfected the Subsidiary Alliance system. Under this treaty, an Indian ruler had to disband his own army and pay for the maintenance of British troops stationed in his territory. He also had to expel all other Europeans (like the French) and accept a British 'Resident' in his court. In return, the British promised to protect him from external attacks.
DECOY BUSTING: Dalhousie pioneered the 'Doctrine of Lapse'. Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General (associated with the Rohilla War). 
EXAM INSIGHT: The Nizam of Hyderabad was the first Indian ruler to accept the Subsidiary Alliance in 1798. It effectively stripped Indian rulers of their foreign policy and military independence.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Under Lord Dalhousie's infamous 'Doctrine of Lapse', which was the first princely state to be annexed by the British in 1848?

options.option_text: Satara
Jhansi
Awadh
Nagpur

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Doctrine of Lapse stated that if an Indian ruler of a "dependent" state died without a natural biological male heir, his adopted son would NOT be recognized as the legal successor to the throne (though he could inherit private property). The state would "lapse" to the British. Satara (in Maharashtra) was the very first victim of this policy in 1848.
DECOY BUSTING: Jhansi was annexed later in 1853 (leading to Rani Lakshmibai's rebellion). Awadh was annexed in 1856, but notably NOT under the Doctrine of Lapse—it was annexed on the false pretext of "misgovernance" (maladministration).
EXAM INSIGHT: The anger caused by the Doctrine of Lapse among the deposed nobility was a massive political trigger for the Great Revolt of 1857.

questions.stem: The Ryotwari Settlement, under which peasants paid land revenue directly to the state without a zamindari intermediary, was first systematically implemented in which region of British India?

options.option_text: Bengal Presidency under Lord Cornwallis in 1793
Madras Presidency under Thomas Munro around 1820
Bombay Presidency under Mountstuart Elphinstone
North-West Provinces under Holt Mackenzie in 1822

questions.explanation: Thomas Munro pioneered and championed the Ryotwari system in Madras Presidency, where each cultivator held a direct patta (title) from the state and paid revenue based on soil assessment. Bombay later adopted a similar system under Elphinstone, but Madras was the origin. The North-West Provinces are associated with the Mahalwari system, not Ryotwari.

questions.stem: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878, widely condemned as the 'Gagging Act', was passed under Viceroy Lord Lytton to suppress Indian-language newspapers. Which Viceroy repealed it just four years later?

options.option_text: Lord Dufferin, who faced the formation of the Indian National Congress
Lord Ripon, who also introduced Local Self-Government reforms in 1882
Lord Lansdowne, who dealt with the Age of Consent controversy in 1891
Lord Curzon, who later partitioned Bengal in 1905 for administrative reasons

questions.explanation: Lord Ripon repealed the Vernacular Press Act in 1882, earning him immense goodwill among Indians. He was a liberal Viceroy who simultaneously introduced Local Self-Government (1882), laying the basis for municipal and district boards. Lord Dufferin is a common distractor because he presided over the founding of the INC in 1885, but that was after Ripon's tenure ended.

questions.stem: The Ilbert Bill of 1883, introduced during Lord Ripon's viceroyalty, triggered violent European protests in India because it proposed that qualified Indian magistrates could try which category of persons in mofussil (non-presidency) areas?

options.option_text: Indian zamindars charged with revenue evasion under civil law
European British subjects in criminal proceedings outside presidency towns
Native Indian soldiers accused of insubordination under military codes
Indian merchants disputing customs duties levied by British port officials

questions.explanation: The Ilbert Bill sought to remove a racial anomaly whereby Indian ICS officers (district judges/collectors) could not try European British subjects in criminal cases outside Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras. European planters and settlers launched the 'White Mutiny', forcing a compromise in 1884 that allowed Europeans to demand a jury with at least half European members. The episode exposed the racial hierarchy entrenched in colonial law.

questions.stem: The Hunter Commission (Indian Education Commission) of 1882, appointed to review the progress of Wood's Despatch of 1854, made its most consequential recommendation regarding which tier of education?

options.option_text: Expanding university education by establishing new Indian universities
Handing over primary and secondary education to provincial and local bodies
Introducing compulsory technical training for Indian artisans and craftsmen
Standardising the medium of instruction as English across all Indian schools

questions.explanation: The Hunter Commission found that the government had concentrated on higher education at the expense of mass literacy. Its central recommendation was to devolve primary and secondary education to newly created municipal and district boards under Lord Ripon's Local Self-Government framework, making grassroots bodies responsible for vernacular schooling. University expansion is a distractor because the focus of the 1857 Universities Acts was already on affiliating institutions, not founding new ones.

questions.stem: Pitt's India Act of 1784 created a 'dual system' of control over the East India Company's Indian territories. What was the precise role of the Board of Control established by this Act?

options.option_text: The Court of Proprietors with veto power over all Indian expenditure
A Board of Control consisting of Cabinet ministers and Privy Councillors
A Select Committee of Parliament with powers to dismiss the Governor-General
The India Office, a Cabinet department replacing the Company's Court of Directors

questions.explanation: Pitt's India Act established a six-member Board of Control (including the Secretary of State and Chancellor of the Exchequer) to supervise the Company's civil, military, and revenue affairs, while the Court of Directors retained commercial functions. This 'dual government' lasted until 1858. The India Office is a deliberate distractor — it replaced the Company after the 1857 revolt, not in 1784. A Select Committee had no such permanent executive power.

questions.stem: The Arms Act of 1878, passed by Viceroy Lord Lytton, made it an offence for Indians to possess firearms without a licence. Which group was explicitly exempted from this prohibition, revealing the racial stratification embedded in British colonial legislation?

options.option_text: Zamindars holding land assessed above fifty rupees annual revenue
Sikh soldiers registered in the British Indian Army under specific regiments
European British subjects and those of European descent by birth
Rulers of princely states allied to the British Crown under subsidiary treaties

questions.explanation: The Arms Act 1878 explicitly exempted European British subjects and Eurasians from its licensing requirement, while disarming the Indian population. This racial double-standard became a rallying point in nationalist discourse; Bal Gangadhar Tilak cited it as proof of the Crown's intent to permanently subjugate Indians. The distractor about Sikh soldiers is plausible because martial-race theory gave Sikhs military privileges, but the statutory exemption was on the basis of European descent, not religion or military service.

questions.stem: The Mahalwari revenue settlement, introduced in the North-Western Provinces and later Punjab, was structurally distinct from both Zamindari and Ryotwari systems in that the primary unit of revenue assessment and responsibility was:

options.option_text: Individual cultivators assessed annually by field-by-field soil measurement
Hereditary zamindars who then sub-let land to tenants at rack-rent rates
The village community collectively, with the mahal (estate/village) as the unit
Local chieftains who paid a fixed tribute and managed internal land disputes

questions.explanation: Under the Mahalwari system (pioneered by Holt Mackenzie in 1822 and refined by James Thomason in the 1840s), the mahal — the village or estate held by a body of co-sharers — was assessed as a whole. The co-sharers were jointly and severally responsible for the revenue demand, with the lambardar (village headman) paying into the treasury. This differs from Ryotwari, where the individual ryot is the unit (Option A), and from Zamindari, where a single landlord holds the patta (Option B). Chieftain-based tribute is associated with pre-British arrangements and not a formal British settlement category.
